newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians closely watch Netanyahu crisis.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians closely watch Netanyahu crisis.

text.p: Palestinians on Thursday closely watched news of a scandal that threatened the political future of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu but were careful to stay out of the Jewish state's internal affairs.

Israeli police confirmed on Wednesday that they had recommended that Netanyahu be indicted for fraud and breach of trust over his ill-fated and short-lived appointment of an attorney general in January.
The recommendation cast a shadow over the latest mission by U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross to revive stalled Israeli-PLO peace talks.
"The president does not intervene in an internal Israeli affair, but he is following the news like everybody else," Ahmed Tibi, an adviser to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat told Reuters.
Nabil Shaath, Minister of Planning and International Cooperation, told Israel Radio: "It's an entirely internal matter for the Israelis."

Arafat aide Nabil Abu Rdainah told Reuters Ross handed Arafat a letter from U.S. President Bill Clinton on Wednesday night reiterating Washington's commitment to work to find a way to get peace talks going again.

Peace negotiations, which have gone on since 1991 and resulted in the handover of most of the Gaza Strip and parts of the West Bank to Palestinian rule, ground to a halt after Netanyahu sent bulldozers on March 18 to begin work on a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
Tibi said that Ross, who had meetings with Netanyahu, Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy and Defence Minister Yithzak Mordechai on Thursday, would meet Arafat again on Thursday night.
"If Ross's initiative does not include freezing settlement activity, particularly on Jabal Abu Ghneim, then such an initiative will not succeed," Tibi said of the Jerusalem construction.
Asked about the impact of the Israeli police recommendation on efforts to revive peace talks, Tibi said:
"Renewing the negotiating has to do with the reasons which caused the crisis and is not related to the Israeli police recommendations, no matter how serious they are."
Netanyahu's lawyer and spokesmen dismissed the charges as baseless and talked of a political smear campaign.
The present attorney general is not bound to accept the police recommendations.

While most Palestinian officials refrained from commenting on the affair, a Palestinian legislator who has been leading a tent vigil near the East Jersualem settlement building site welcomed Netanyahu's homefront troubles.
"I think it's about time that somebody should come in to stop (him) and to come from the Israeli police, that is adequate," said Salah al-Taamari, speaking English.
"I think he's the worst prime minister in Israel and somebody should have stopped him a long time ago," he said.

The right-wing Netanyahu took power in June after ousting Labour party leader Shimon Peres, the architect of Palestinian- Israeli peace deals, in May elections by less than a percentage point. When in opposition, Netanyahu opposed the peace deals.
